terms: A sensor in every phone that measures how fast the phone is speeding up or slowing down in three directions (x, y, z). It also feels gravity, so it knows which way is down.
Units of acceleration. 1 g is the pull of gravity, about 9.81 m/s². A phone lying still reads 1 g.
A short slice of the sensor stream (here 4 seconds). We classify one window at a time.
A single number that summarises a window, for example the average or how much the signal wiggles. The model learns from features, not raw readings.
A program that learned from labelled examples how to guess the activity for a new window.
300 small decision trees that each vote on the answer; the majority wins. Robust and needs little tuning.
The dumbest sensible guess (always predict the most common activity). A real model must beat it.
Precision: when the model says Walking, how often is it right? Recall: of all the real Walking windows, how many did it find?
F1 combines precision and recall into one score. Macro F1 averages it over all six activities equally, so small activities such as Standing count as much as Walking.
Testing on people the model never saw in training, like a real user installing the app.
A grid of actual activity (rows) against predicted activity (columns). The diagonal is correct answers.
Showing the model labelled examples so it finds the patterns itself. Done once, takes about a minute.
Asking the finished model about a new window. No learning happens; it takes about 30 ms.
A flowchart of yes/no questions about the features that ends in an activity, like twenty questions.
When a model memorises its training data. Ours scores 100% on its training windows but 85% on unseen people, so we report the 85%.
The saved trained model on disk: models/activity_model.joblib, about 22 MB. It is binary; python -m mlengine.describe shows what is inside.
The Python server behind the demo page. The page asks it for a window and it returns the prediction as JSON.

slides.title: Title
slides.say: Good day. I am Moses, and with me are Collins and Kathy. Our project is a machine learning engine that looks at the motion sensor in a phone and works out what the person is doing, and it can also raise a warning if it looks like they have fallen. I will cover the problem and the data, Collins will explain how we prepared the data and tested it fairly, and Kathy will present the results and the fall detection. I will close with the conclusion.

slides.title: The problem and our goal
slides.say: The problem: falls are a major cause of injury for elderly people, and the longer help takes to arrive, the worse the outcome. Almost everyone carries a smartphone, and every smartphone has an accelerometer, which is a sensor that measures movement in three directions. So the hardware is already there. Our goal has two parts, shown in the table. First, a classifier that says which of six activities the person is doing: walking, jogging, going upstairs, going downstairs, sitting or standing. Second, a fall rule that looks for a hard impact followed by the person staying still.
slides.on_slide: Two short points on why falls matter, and a table of the two parts of the engine.

slides.title: How machine learning works here
slides.on_slide: A two-part diagram: learning (done once) on top, using the saved model (every new window) below, plus two short points.
slides.say: Before the details, here is what machine learning means in this project. Normally to build a program you write the rules yourself. We could not realistically write rules for what walking looks like in a stream of numbers. So we did the opposite: we gave the computer thousands of examples where the answer is already known, and it worked out the rules itself. That is supervised learning. The top row is the learning stage. Our examples are 25,230 four-second windows, each labelled with the real activity, because the volunteers in the WISDM study told the researchers what they were doing. A training algorithm searches for patterns that separate the activities, and the result is a model, which is simply a file on disk. Ours is called activity_model.joblib and holds 300 decision trees. Training happens once and takes about a minute. The bottom row is the using stage. A new window arrives with no label. We compute the same 32 features and ask the saved model, which answers in about 30 milliseconds, with a confidence. No learning happens at this point. The model is only being used. A window arrives every two seconds, so this is comfortably fast enough to run live.

slides.title: The pipeline
slides.say: This diagram is the whole project in one picture, read left to right. We start with the raw data file from the WISDM dataset. We clean it, because real sensor files contain broken lines. We cut the continuous stream into short windows. We turn each window into a handful of summary numbers, called features. We train models on those features and save the best one. The saved model tells us the activity, and separately the fall rule checks the same window for a fall. Everything is written as a small Python package so it can be re-run with one command.
slides.on_slide: A flow diagram: raw file, clean, windows, features, train, model, then activity and fall rule.

slides.title: The WISDM dataset
slides.say: We used a public dataset called WISDM from Fordham University. 36 volunteers kept an Android phone in their front trouser pocket and did the six activities while the phone recorded movement 20 times every second. After cleaning we have just over a million readings. The chart shows they are not evenly spread: walking and jogging are about two thirds of the data, while sitting and standing are small. That imbalance matters later, because it means accuracy alone can flatter a model, so we also report a fairer score called macro F1.
slides.on_slide: Four stat cards (36 subjects, 20 Hz, 1,019,496 readings, 6 activities) and a bar chart of readings per activity.

slides.title: Data exploration (Deliverable 1)
slides.say: This is our first deliverable, where we examined the raw file. It has 1,086,466 rows and 6 columns: the subject, the activity, a timestamp, and the x, y, z acceleration. The IDs and timestamps are integers, the activity is text, and the three acceleration values are decimals. It is almost complete: exactly one value is missing, a single z reading, and a few lines in the file were malformed, so we skip them. Our cleaning step removes bad lines, missing values, readings with a zero timestamp and duplicates. That takes 1,086,466 down to 1,019,496 readings, about 6 percent removed.
slides.on_slide: A table answering the Deliverable 1 questions (rows/columns, datatypes, completeness, df_sample) and the cleaning numbers.
slides.handoff: That is the data and where we started. Collins will now explain how we turned it into something a model can learn from.

slides.title: What the signals look like
slides.say: Here is four seconds of movement for each activity. The vertical axis is the total strength of the acceleration. Notice how different they look: jogging swings hard, walking has a steady rhythm, and sitting and standing are almost flat lines. That tells us the problem is learnable. It also warns us that upstairs, downstairs and walking look alike, and we will see that is exactly where the model struggles.
slides.on_slide: Six small line graphs, one per activity, showing four seconds of acceleration.

slides.title: Windowing: turning a stream into examples
slides.say: A single reading, one instant of acceleration, tells you almost nothing, because walking, running and sitting down can all produce the same number for a split second. What identifies an activity is how the signal behaves over a few seconds. So we cut the stream into windows of 80 readings, which is 4 seconds. Each new window starts 2 seconds after the last, so they overlap by half. That gives us more examples and stops an event being cut in two by bad luck. We only keep windows where one person is doing one activity, so each has a single correct label. This gives us 25,230 labelled windows.
slides.on_slide: A diagram of overlapping windows and three bullets with the window size and count.

slides.title: Features: summarising each window
slides.say: A window is 240 raw numbers, which is too much and too noisy to learn from directly. So we summarise each window into 32 features. The averages tell us the phone's orientation, which is how sitting differs from standing, since gravity pulls along different axes. The spread and range tell us how vigorous the movement is. The frequency features tell us how fast the movement repeats, which separates walking from jogging. You do not need to memorise the table; the point is that each feature captures one idea about how the person is moving.
slides.on_slide: A table of the six feature groups: what each measures and why it helps.

slides.title: A decision tree: twenty questions
slides.on_slide: A real decision tree from our model, drawn two levels deep, with the question at each step.
slides.say: Now let us look inside the model. A decision tree is like a game of twenty questions. This is the top of a real tree from our trained model, not a drawing we made up. The first question is: how much does the phone's up-and-down reading wiggle? That feature is called y_mad. If it wiggles very little, the person is barely moving, and the next question separates sitting from standing, using the highest up-and-down reading. In the training data that branch was 100 percent sitting for one group and 93 percent standing for the other. If it wiggles a lot, the next question looks at the vibration energy. Low energy leads to a mixed group where downstairs is only 33 percent, so the real tree keeps asking more questions further down. High energy leads to jogging, 88 percent pure. Two things to remember. First, nobody chose these questions. The training algorithm tried many questions and kept the ones that best split the labelled examples. Second, a real tree is much deeper than this picture: on average more than 25 levels, with around a thousand end points each. We only show the top.

slides.title: A forest: 300 trees vote
slides.on_slide: Two bar charts showing how the 300 trees voted on a real Walking window and on a real Downstairs window that was mispredicted.
slides.say: One tree alone can be wrong, and a tree grown on all the data tends to memorise it. So we grow 300 trees. Each is trained on a random sample of the windows and looks at random subsets of the features, so they make different mistakes. To classify a window, all 300 trees give their answer and we combine them. That is a random forest. Left: a real walking window from someone the model never saw. About 167 of the 300 trees said Walking, with the others split between Downstairs and Upstairs. Walking wins clearly, and the confidence percentage the app shows comes from this agreement. Right: a real downstairs window that the model got wrong. The vote was close: 112 trees said Upstairs, 99 said Walking and 88 said Downstairs. A close vote means low confidence, which is why the app says 'likely' instead of sounding certain. One honest point. If we test the forest on the same windows it trained on, it scores 100 percent, because it has effectively memorised them. On people it has never seen it scores 85 percent. That gap is called overfitting. It is normal for random forests, and it is exactly why we test on unseen people and report the 85 percent as our real result.

slides.title: Evaluating honestly: subject-wise split
slides.say: This slide is about testing fairly. The obvious approach is to shuffle all the windows and set some aside for testing. But windows from the same person are nearly identical, so the model would effectively see the test answers during training and the score would be inflated. A real user is a new person, so we hold out whole people: 27 subjects for training and 9 completely unseen subjects for testing. We compared three models: a baseline that always guesses the most common activity, logistic regression, and a random forest. We report accuracy, and macro F1, which treats all six activities equally.
slides.on_slide: A diagram of the train/test split (27 train subjects, 9 test subjects) and the three models and metrics.
slides.handoff: So that is how we prepared the data and tested it fairly. Kathy will now show how well it works.

slides.title: Results
slides.say: The baseline gets 39 percent accuracy just by always guessing walking, and a macro F1 of only 0.09. Both real models are far better. The random forest is the best, with 85 percent accuracy and macro F1 of 0.775, on people it has never seen. To be sure that was not a lucky split, we repeated the test five times with different groups of people and got a macro F1 of 0.79, give or take 0.035. So the result is stable. The random forest is the model we saved. One thing to flag: on its own training windows the forest scores 100 percent, but on unseen people 85 percent. That gap is overfitting, which is why we trust only the unseen-people number.
slides.on_slide: A bar chart and table comparing the three models, plus the cross-validation result.

slides.title: Where the model succeeds and struggles
slides.say: The confusion matrix shows, for each real activity on the left, what the model predicted along the top. The diagonal is correct answers. Jogging and walking are excellent. The weak spot is downstairs: only 34 percent of real downstairs windows are found, and most are labelled upstairs or walking. That makes sense, because with a phone in a pocket these three movements are physically very similar. Sitting and standing are also sometimes swapped, since neither involves movement and they differ mainly in phone tilt. We are reporting this openly rather than hiding it.
slides.on_slide: The confusion matrix and a table of precision, recall and F1 per activity.

slides.title: Fall-risk detection
slides.say: An important honest point: the WISDM dataset contains no falls, so we could not train a fall detector from it. Instead we wrote a rule based on physics. A fall has two stages: a hard impact, then the person lies still. The rule flags a window if the peak acceleration is at least 2.5 g and the last half second is almost perfectly still at about 1 g. Left graph: a real walking window. It crosses 2.5 g on some footsteps, but the person keeps moving, so no flag. Right graph: a simulated fall, a spike then stillness, which is flagged. The caveat is that we only tested it on a simulated signal, so before real use it must be validated on a dataset with real falls.
slides.on_slide: Two graphs: a real walking window (no flag) and a simulated fall (flagged), plus three bullets.

slides.title: Live demonstration
slides.on_slide: Left: a screenshot of the demo (the backup if the live demo cannot run). Right: the four things we will do live.
slides.say: Now let us see it working. Collins is running our demo, which looks like a real app. The left phone is Mary's phone, the one that does the sensing. The right phone is her caregiver's phone, for example a daughter or son. I will explain what we see. Every activity you will see is a real four-second recording from one of nine people the model never saw during training. [Collins clicks Walk, then Jog.] On Mary's phone the model names what she is doing and says how sure it is. The caregiver's phone updates at the same moment and keeps a simple activity history. Notice that nobody on the caregiver side sees raw numbers, just plain language. [Collins clicks Stairs down two or three times.] This is our weak spot. If the model is not sure, the app says 'likely' and shows the percentage instead of pretending to be certain. [Collins clicks Simulate a fall.] This is staged: a hard impact, then a motionless phone. Mary's phone asks 'Are you OK?' with a ten second countdown, so a dropped phone does not frighten the family. If she answers, the alert is cancelled. If she does not answer, or presses help, the caregiver gets an urgent notification. [Collins ticks Technical view.] For those who want the evidence, this panel shows the sensor signal, the model's confidence for each activity, and the fall rule's numbers. [Optional: Collins clicks Play a day.] This plays a whole day automatically, ending in a fall.
slides.handoff: Moses will now show what is running behind it.

slides.title: Under the hood
slides.on_slide: A table of the code files and what each does, plus key facts about the saved model and the demo's backend.
slides.say: This slide is for anyone who wants to know what is actually running behind the demo. The code is a small Python package with five parts: data cleaning, features, training, prediction, and the demo server. The trained model is a file on disk in the models folder. It holds 300 decision trees, roughly 800,000 decision points in total, which take 22 megabytes. It is not on GitHub because it is large and can be recreated in about a minute with one command. The demo works like this: the page in the browser asks our local Python server for a window of data. The server picks a real recording from people the model never trained on, computes the 32 features, asks the saved model, runs the fall rule, and sends the answer back as JSON. The browser then draws the two phone screens. In a real product, the model would run either on the phone itself or on a small server that receives the sensor data. If asked, we can show the code and run it live.
slides.handoff: Kathy will now cover the limitations.

slides.title: Limitations and future work
slides.say: These are the things we would fix next. The fall rule is unvalidated and needs real fall data, such as the SisFall or MobiAct datasets. WISDM has no lying-down activity, which matters after a fall. The volunteers were not elderly, so we cannot promise the same accuracy for the target users. All the data came from a trouser pocket. Downstairs is weak. And finally this is currently a Python library, not yet a phone app. Being clear about these limits is part of doing the work properly.
slides.on_slide: A table of limitations paired with next steps.
slides.handoff: Those are the limits. I will hand back to Moses to wrap up.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.say: To summarise: our engine recognises six everyday activities with about 85 percent accuracy on people it has never seen, compared with 39 percent for the simple baseline. Because we cleaned the data carefully and tested on unseen people, those numbers are a realistic estimate rather than an inflated one. On top of that sits a transparent fall rule, and we have been clear about what has and has not been validated. Anyone can reproduce all of it with one command. Thank you, and we are happy to take questions. Each of us will answer questions about our own part.
slides.on_slide: Three summary points and the reference.

qa: Why not just use accuracy?
The data is imbalanced. Always guessing Walking is already right about 39% of the time. Macro F1 gives every activity equal weight, so it exposes weak classes like Downstairs.
Kathy
Why did you split by person instead of randomly?
Neighbouring windows from the same person are almost identical. A random split lets the model memorise a person, giving an inflated score. Splitting by person tests whether it works on a new user.
Collins
Why a random forest?
It handles many features, captures non-linear patterns, needs little tuning, and gave the best macro F1 of the three models we compared.
Collins
Is the fall detection proven?
No, and we say so. WISDM has no falls. It is a physics-based rule tested only on a simulated signal. It needs validation on real fall data before real use.
Kathy
Why is downstairs bad?
It looks very much like walking and upstairs when the phone is in a pocket. 34% recall; most errors go to Upstairs and Walking.
Kathy
What does 1 g or 9.81 mean?
The acceleration due to gravity. A still phone reads about 9.81 m/s², i.e. 1 g.
Moses
Why 4-second windows with 50% overlap?
4 seconds contains several steps, so the rhythm is visible. Overlap gives more examples and avoids cutting an event in half.
Collins
How many rows were removed in cleaning and why?
About 67,000 of 1,086,466 (6.2%): malformed or missing values, zero timestamps (clock not started) and duplicates.
Moses
Will it work for elderly people?
Unknown. The volunteers were not elderly and elderly gait differs. Testing on elderly participants is a next step.
Kathy
How do I run it?
python -m mlengine.train trains and saves the model; python -m mlengine.predict readings.csv classifies a window.
Moses
Is the demo using real data?
The activity windows are real four-second recordings from the nine held-out subjects. The fall is staged, because the dataset has no falls.
Collins
Why did the model get that one wrong?
Downstairs is our weakest class (34% recall); it looks like Upstairs and Walking from a pocket phone. The scoreboard shows errors openly on purpose.
Kathy
Could this run on a real phone?
Not yet. The demo runs on a laptop. The next step is to wrap the model in a phone app or a small service that streams sensor data.
Moses
Where is the model stored?

In the models folder: models/activity_model.joblib (about 22 MB) is the deployed one, and models/demo_model.joblib (about 16 MB) is the one used by the demo. They are not on GitHub because they are large and can be recreated with python -m mlengine.train.
Moses
What is inside the model file?

A Python dictionary saved with joblib: the trained random forest (300 trees, roughly 800,000 nodes) and the list of the 32 feature names in the order the model expects. It is binary, so run python -m mlengine.describe to read it as text (it also saves models/model_summary.txt).
Moses
How does the app get a prediction?

The page asks our Python server for a window. The server computes the 32 features, loads the saved model, gets the probabilities for the six activities, runs the fall rule and returns it all as JSON. About 30 ms.
Moses
How would this run on a real phone?

Either the model is exported to run on the phone itself (for example in a mobile format such as TensorFlow Lite or ONNX), or the phone sends windows to a small server. Neither is built yet; the demo runs on a laptop.
Moses
What is training, and how long does it take?
Showing the model labelled windows so it learns the patterns. About a minute on a laptop. It is done once, not on every prediction.
Collins
Is this deep learning?

No. It is classical machine learning: hand-designed features and a random forest. That was a deliberate choice for a dataset of this size: it trains in a minute, runs fast, and we can explain each decision. Deep learning on the raw signal is a future option.
Collins
Why does it score 100% on training data but 85% on test data?
The forest memorises its training windows (overfitting). That gap is normal for random forests. It is why we never report training accuracy and always test on people the model has never seen.
Collins
How do you know it is not overfitting?

We test on 9 people who are completely held out, and we repeat with 5-fold cross-validation grouped by person: macro F1 0.791 plus or minus 0.035. The scores are stable across different groups of people.
Collins
What does the model look at most?

The orientation and spread of the up-down axis: z_mean, y_mad, y_energy, y_std and the min and max of y. That matches the physics: orientation separates sitting from standing, and vibration separates moving activities.
Collins
What libraries did you use?

Deliberately few. The engine needs only numpy (arrays and the FFT) and scikit-learn (the models and joblib for saving them); everything else is the Python standard library, including the demo's web server. pandas, matplotlib and reportlab are only used for the optional notebook and for building the report, not by the engine.
Moses
Could the model keep learning from users?
Not as built. It is trained once. Improving it means collecting more labelled data (ideally from elderly users) and retraining.
Kathy
What about false alarms?
The fall rule needs both an impact and stillness, and the app asks 'Are you OK?' for 10 seconds before alerting the family. Real false-alarm rates are unknown until the rule is tested on real falls.
Kathy
Why use scikit-learn instead of writing the model yourselves?

The model is the standard, well-tested part, and re-implementing a random forest would add risk and no insight. What we wrote ourselves is what is specific to this problem: cleaning, windowing, the 32 features, the subject-wise testing and the fall rule. We can explain every one of those line by line.
Moses
